questions.prompt: Emna will spend two months next summer inside an engineering company in Sousse, working with the team and without pay, to learn how the job is really done. Her cousin tells her to call that period "a stage" in the letter she is writing in English. Which word does English use for it?

options.text: an internship
a stage
a scholarship
a training course

questions.explanation: "an internship" is the word English uses: a period spent inside a company, doing the work itself in order to learn it, is an internship, whether it is paid or not. "a stage" is the word your own language lends you, and English keeps it for something else entirely: a stage is one step in a process, or the platform an actor stands on, so an English reader would picture a theatre and not a company. "a scholarship" is money given to a student so that studying costs the family nothing; nobody is giving Emna money, she is giving her time. And "a training course" is a course you follow to be taught the job, with a teacher and a programme; Emna is not sitting in a course, she is inside the company doing the work.

questions.prompt: Wassim's little sister leaves the nursery at six, and every Thursday he goes there and brings her home. He writes the sentence in his English notebook with the verb of the lesson. Which line is correct?

options.text: Every Thursday I pick up her at six.
Every Thursday I pick her at six.
Every Thursday I pick her up at six.
Every Thursday I pick up she at six.

questions.explanation: "Every Thursday I pick her up at six." is the correct line: pick up is a verb in two pieces, and when what you collect is a pronoun, the pronoun goes between the two pieces. That is why the lesson prints the verb as pick somebody up, with the person written inside it. "Every Thursday I pick up her at six." keeps the order you may use with a noun, pick up my sister, and applies it to a pronoun, where English does not allow it. "Every Thursday I pick up she at six." makes a second mistake on top of the first: she is a subject pronoun, and after a verb the object form her is needed. And "Every Thursday I pick her at six." drops the little word up, and with it the meaning: pick alone means to choose, or to gather fruit, so the sentence would say that he chooses his sister every Thursday.

questions.prompt: For two years Mouna spent every Saturday at the swimming pool in Sfax. She stopped last September, and since the start of this school year she has spent her Saturdays at the town library. She wants to tell her new classmates what her Saturdays are like now. Which sentence does she say?

options.text: I used to go to the library on Saturdays.
I usually go to the library on Saturdays.
I would go to the library on Saturdays.
I am used to go to the library on Saturdays.

questions.explanation: "I usually go to the library on Saturdays." is what Mouna means: the present simple with usually is how English states a habit you have now, and the library Saturdays are this year's habit. "I used to go to the library on Saturdays." says the exact opposite: used to always announces that the habit is finished, so her classmates would understand that she has stopped going, which is true of the swimming pool and not of the library. "I would go to the library on Saturdays." sends the sentence into the past as well: would tells a repeated action inside a past that has already been set up, and it can never describe what somebody does this year. And "I am used to go to the library on Saturdays." mixes two structures: be used to means that something has stopped feeling strange, it is followed by a noun or an -ing form, so it would have to be am used to going, and even then it would say how she feels about her Saturdays, not what she does with them.

questions.prompt: Nizar wrote the club's timetable in big letters and pinned it by the door. His aim was that the new members should be able to read it from the yard, without coming in. Which sentence gives that aim?

options.text: He pinned the timetable by the door to read it from the yard.
He pinned the timetable by the door for that the new members could read it from the yard.
He pinned the timetable by the door so that to be read from the yard.
He pinned the timetable by the door so that the new members could read it from the yard.

questions.explanation: "He pinned the timetable by the door so that the new members could read it from the yard." is the sentence: the person who is meant to do the second action is not Nizar but the new members, and an infinitive cannot carry a second person, so the aim has to be given by a clause with so that; the main verb is a past, which is why the modal inside the clause is could and not can. "He pinned the timetable by the door to read it from the yard." is correct English but says something else: an infinitive of purpose always attaches to the subject of the sentence, so this line means that Nizar pinned it up in order to read it himself, which is not why anybody pins a timetable to a door. "He pinned the timetable by the door for that the new members could read it from the yard." copies the link word of your own language straight into English, where for that introduces nothing at all. And "He pinned the timetable by the door so that to be read from the yard." keeps so that and then gives it an infinitive; so that opens a clause, and a clause needs a subject and a verb of its own.

questions.prompt: A small clinic in Bizerte is printing a card that tells visitors who does what. Three lines are right and one has been written with the wrong word in it. Which line is wrong?

options.text: The diplomat takes the patients' blood pressure before the check-up.
The physician's assistant does part of the doctor's routine work beside him.
The physician examines the patients and decides on the treatment.
The clerk keeps the records and answers the telephone at the counter.

questions.explanation: "The diplomat takes the patients' blood pressure before the check-up." is the wrong line: a diplomat is the person who represents his country abroad, in an embassy, and he has no place on the staff card of a clinic; the line needs a nurse or the doctor's assistant. "The physician examines the patients and decides on the treatment." is right, because a physician is a doctor of medicine. "The physician's assistant does part of the doctor's routine work beside him." is right too: that is exactly what the job of the listening lesson is, and it is why it takes years of study of its own. And "The clerk keeps the records and answers the telephone at the counter." is right as well, since a clerk is an employee who does office work, in a clinic as in any other office.
